rows.what: Loads configs/models/<name>.yml on top of base.yml. Any key that file sets cannot also be set on the command line with a different value unless override_model_config=true (measured error on the Reading tab).
rows.comment: override config settings to match a specific model. other than the override, nothing should use this!

rows.what: Which decoder layer class the decoder stacks: one of 25 DecoderBlockType values (llama2, gemma3, deepseek, qwen3, gpt3, ...). The running example is the gpt3 block: LayerNorm with bias, biased projections, learned positions.
rows.comment: which style of decoderblock to use.

rows.what: Residual width d_model (multiplied by global_parameter_scale, 1 by default, to give emb_dim).
Number of query heads.
Number of key/value heads; fewer than query heads gives grouped-query attention. The gpt3 block asserts they are equal.
Hidden width of the MLP (per expert for MoE models use base_moe_mlp_dim).
Number of decoder layers; with scan_layers they are stacked into one array per weight.
Width of each attention head; MaxText sets it explicitly rather than deriving emb_dim / heads.
Activation per MLP input projection: ['silu','linear'] is SwiGLU (two input matrices, one gated); ['gelu'] is one matrix with jax.nn.gelu, which defaults to the tanh approximation.
Vocabulary size. It must divide by the mesh axes that shard it (the vocab rule maps to tensor axes): the running example's 65 cannot be split 4 ways.
rows.comment: powers of 2 for sharding
rows.above: Tokenizer

rows.what: Epsilon of RMSNorm or LayerNorm; 1e-5 here, PyTorch's LayerNorm default too.
rows.comment: epsilon value for rmsnorm, layernorm.

rows.what: Tie the output head to the token embedding (true) or keep a separate logits_dense kernel (false).
A positive value adds learned absolute position embeddings of that length (GPT-3 style); -1 means none (RoPE models).
rows.comment: enable gpt3 position embedding with a positive trainable_position_size

rows.what: One projection producing q, k and v together (a [embed, 3, heads, head_dim] kernel) instead of three.
rows.above: Combine matmuls for QKV and MLP

rows.what: Experts per MoE layer; 1 means a dense model.
rows.above: mixture of experts (moe)

rows.what: Top-k routing: experts each token is sent to.
Expert capacity for token dropping; -1 (default) means dropless, with ragged all-to-all and grouped matmul instead of padding.
rows.comment: a factor to decide expert capacity for token dropping, and no dropping by default

rows.what: Activation and matmul dtype: bfloat16 by default.
rows.above: activation dtypes.

rows.what: Dtype of the stored parameters (and so of the optimizer's master copy): float32 by default.
rows.above: global parameter scale needs to be a power of 2. if you want finer grained control of the model sizes then you should explicitly set base_embed_dim, base_num_query_heads, base_num_kv_heads, base_mlp_dim, base_num_decoder_layers and/or head_dim.

rows.what: Dtype gradients are cast to after value_and_grad, before clipping and the update.
rows.above: gradient dtype

rows.what: Passed to the dots: default, high or highest. On TPU 'default' runs float32 matmuls in bfloat16 passes; on CPU it changes nothing (the runs here set highest for exact comparisons).
rows.above: choose one of default, high, and highest. https://kolonist26-jax-kr.readthedocs.io/en/latest/jax.lax.html#jax.lax.precision

rows.what: Cast the logits to float32 before the loss.
rows.comment: whether to cast the logits to fp32. the higher precision is generally beneficial, but it can vary slightly.

rows.what: '' for none, or int8, fp8 variants and others through AQT or Qwix.
rows.above: 'int8' for dynamic range quantization using 8-bits 'intmp' for mixed precision quantization for inference as described here: src/maxtext/configs/quantization/readme.md 'fp8' for 8-bit floating-point gemms on nvidia gpus. 'nanoo_fp8' for 8-bit floating-point gemms on amd mi300/mi325 gpus. 'fp8_full' for fp8 quantization with static scaling. 'serve_fp8_weight' to load and use FP8 checkpoint directly at inference time.

rows.what: Run the decoder layers with jax.lax.scan over weights stacked on a 'layers' axis: compile time and HLO size stop growing with depth (measured on the Reading tab).
rows.above: Whether to use jax.lax.scan over layers (stacked/unstacked checkpoint). We recommend setting this to false when using pipeline parallelism, instead scanning the PP iterations. When resuming from a checkpoint, this flag is auto-determined from metadata.

rows.what: Which axis of each stacked weight is the layer axis: 1, so a [embed, mlp] kernel becomes [embed, layers, mlp]. The scan moves it to axis 0 at run time.

What the backward pass may keep from the forward pass of each layer (jax.checkpoint policy): 'full' keeps only the layer input and recomputes everything else; 'minimal' keeps the projections' outputs.
rows.above: Choose 'remat_policy' between 'minimal_with_context', 'minimal', 'save_dot_with_context_except_mlp', 'save_dot_except_mlpwi', 'save_dot_except_mlp', 'save_qkv_proj', 'qkv_proj_offloaded', 'custom', 'minimal_offloaded', 'save_out_proj' and 'full'. These options offer a trade-off between speed (fastest to slowest) and HBM usage (highest to lowest)

rows.what: Keep optimizer state in host memory and move it to the device for the update.
Accumulate gradients over this many microbatches before one optimizer update.
rows.above: Instead of updating the weights every step, you may effectively use a larger batch by accumulating the gradient over a set of steps.

rows.what: Compute logits and loss in this many tiles to bound peak memory for large vocabularies.
rows.above: Vocab Tiling Configs Enables a memory-saving optimization by computing the cross-entropy loss in chunks. The logits are tiled into `num_vocab_tiling` parts along the batch-sequence axis, reducing peak memory usage. This is highly recommended for models with large vocabularies (e.g., Gemma). Set to a value greater than 1 to enable.

rows.what: Kernel: autoselected, dot_product, flash (splash attention in Pallas on TPU), cudnn_flash_te on GPU. 'autoselected' falls back to dot_product on CPU, for short sequences (under 128) and in decode.
rows.comment: Supported attention: autoselected, dot_product, flash, cudnn_flash_te
rows.above: The attention parameter dictates the specific algorithm/methodology used to compute the attention scores The attention_type parameter determines the variants of attention, e.g. global or local_sliding

rows.what: Variant: global (causal), local_sliding, chunk, mla, full, compressed, block_diffusion.
rows.comment: Supported attention_type: global, local_sliding, chunk, mla, full, compressed, block_diffusion

rows.what: Window for local_sliding attention.
Splash attention query block size (TPU kernel tiling); 512 by default.
rows.above: Splash attention block sizes These can be tuned for specific hardware generations, and can be set up to the model's sequence length.

rows.what: auto: annotations plus GSPMD/Shardy propagation; explicit: sharding in the types (see Sharding and scale).
rows.comment: can be either auto or explicit
rows.above: Parallelism

rows.what: Ordered (logical name, mesh axes) pairs; each array dimension takes the first rule whose mesh axes are still free. A model file's rule replaces every base rule with the same name (llama2-7b.yml sets ['norm', 'fsdp'], so its norm scales are FSDP-sharded instead of split over 'tensor').
FSDP degree inside a slice (over ICI). -1 absorbs every device not used by other axes: on 8 devices with nothing else set, fsdp = 8.
rows.comment: recommended ICI axis to be auto-sharded

rows.what: Pure data parallelism inside a slice (replicated parameters).
Tensor parallelism inside a slice: heads, mlp and vocab dimensions split over 'tensor'.
Expert parallelism inside a slice.
Pipeline stages inside a slice (the 'stage' mesh axis).
Context (sequence) parallelism inside a slice.
Data parallelism across slices over the data-centre network; -1 absorbs the slices.
rows.comment: recommended DCN axis to be auto-sharded

rows.what: Number of TPU slices; -1 lets MaxText count them.
rows.above: Unless explicitly specified, the number of TPU slices is automatically determined. It should only be set for disaggregated reinforcement learning workloads using multiple slices. For ahead of time compilation, you should set compile_toplogy_num_slices, which will in turn set this value. For non-TPU environments this is set to 1.

rows.what: all_gather (default), ring, ulysses or usp.
rows.comment: "all_gather", "ring", "ulysses", or "usp"

rows.what: Microbatches per pipeline step; the bubble is (stages - 1) / (repeats x microbatches + stages - 1) (base.yml:450).
rows.above: num_pipeline_microbatches must be a multiple of the number of pipeline stages. By default it is set to the number of stages. Note the microbatch_size is given by global_batch_size / num_pipeline_microbatches, where global_batch_size = per_device_batch_size * num_devices

rows.what: Largest fraction of parameter bytes allowed to stay unsharded before MaxText raises.
rows.above: sharding tolerance: float between 0.0 and 1.0 representing the allowed percentage of non-sharded parameters.

rows.what: Sequences per device per step; global batch = this x number of devices (12 x 8 = 96 on the 8 simulated devices here). Fractions below 1 are allowed.
rows.above: Dataset

rows.what: Sequence length.
rows.comment: Maximum sequence length

rows.what: Training steps; also the default length of the learning-rate schedule.
rows.comment: If set to -1 then will inherit value from learning_rate_schedule_steps
rows.above: Training loop

rows.what: Peak learning rate (3e-5 by default, a fine-tuning value).
rows.above: 2) Stable phase at [learning_rate] for the majority of training 3) Decay from [learning_rate] to [learning_rate * learning_rate_final_fraction] over [learning_rate_schedule_steps * wsd_decay_steps_fraction] steps The decay can be either linear or cosine based on wsd_decay_style 4) Constant learning rate of 0 from learning_rate_schedule_steps to steps (if steps > learning_rate_schedule_steps)  The zero learning rate section can be used to more accurately measure the fully trained model's performa

rows.what: cosine or wsd (warmup, stable, decay).
rows.comment: Options: 'cosine' or 'wsd'

rows.what: Fraction of the schedule spent in linear warmup, which starts at learning rate 0 at step 0.
rows.comment: Fraction of learning_rate_schedule_steps used for warmup phase (applies to both schedules)

rows.what: Final learning rate as a fraction of the peak (1.0 makes the cosine flat, used here to match the running example).
rows.comment: Final LR as fraction of peak LR (applies to both cosine and WSD schedules)

rows.what: adamw, adam_pax, sgd or muon.
rows.comment: one of "adamw", "adam_pax", "sgd", or "muon"

rows.what: Adam first-moment decay.
rows.comment: Exponential decay rate to track the first moment of past gradients.
rows.above: AdamW optimizer parameters We use AdamW following Llama2's training details, see https://arxiv.org/pdf/2307.09288.pdf section 2.2

rows.what: Adam second-moment decay: 0.95, the Llama 2 value (optax and PyTorch default to 0.999).
rows.comment: Exponential decay rate to track the second moment of past gradients.

rows.what: Adam epsilon, added outside the square root.
rows.comment: A small constant applied to denominator outside of the square root.

rows.what: Decoupled weight decay coefficient.
rows.comment: AdamW Weight decay

rows.what: Regexes of parameter paths NOT to decay. Empty by default, so biases, norm scales and embeddings are decayed too; the run here passed ['bias', 'scale', 'embedding'].
rows.comment: List of parameter names/patterns to exclude from weight decay in AdamW, like ['bias', '.*norm', '.*ln.*'].

rows.what: Global-norm clipping threshold; 0 disables it.
rows.above: You may disable clipping by setting gradient_clipping_threshold to zero.

rows.what: Dropout switch; with it off the run is a deterministic function of the seeds.
rows.above: When dropout is false the model is a deterministic function of the data_shuffle_seed and init_weights_seed (i.e. reproducible losses)

rows.what: Dropout probability (0.0 by default, so dropout does nothing even when enabled).
Weight of the z-loss on the log-partition function (0 by default).
synthetic (default), hf, grain or tfds.
rows.above: dataset_type must be synthetic, hf, grain, tfds details in: https://github.com/AI-Hypercomputer/maxtext/blob/main/docs/guides/data_input_pipeline.md

rows.what: Pack several documents per sequence with segment ids so attention does not cross them.
sentencepiece, tiktoken or huggingface.
rows.comment: Currently supporting: "tiktoken", "sentencepiece", "huggingface"
rows.above: grain and tfds pipeline supports tokenizer_type: sentencepiece, huggingface, tiktoken hf pipeline only supports huggingface type, and will ignore tokenizer_type flag

rows.what: Shuffle the data source.
Seed for parameter initialisation.
Create the Orbax checkpointer. If the run directory already holds a checkpoint, training resumes from it.
rows.above: If enable_checkpointing is true, an asynchronous checkpointer will be used if async_checkpointing is true, else a synchronous one is used. If you have problems with the checkpointer we recommend trying the synchronous one.

rows.what: Write checkpoints in the background while training continues.
Save every this many steps (10,000 by default).
Start from parameters only (no optimizer state), for fine-tuning.
rows.above: Loads a just parameters from a specific directory e.g. gs://my-base-output-directory/my-previous-run-name/checkpoints/items/NUMBER or NUMBER/items

rows.what: Start from a full state: parameters, optimizer state and step.
rows.above: Loads a full checkpoint including optimizer state and step count from a specific directory e.g. gs://my-base-output-directory/my-previous-run-name/checkpoints/items/NUMBER or NUMBER/items

rows.what: How many checkpoints Orbax keeps, through its keep-latest-N preservation policy (common/checkpoint_context.py). The default None was not tested here.
tpu, gpu, gpu_multiprocess or cpu. MaxText's own CPU tests pass cpu, as the runs here do.
rows.comment: Supported hardware types are 'tpu', 'gpu', 'gpu_multiprocess' and 'cpu'
rows.above: Hardware

rows.what: Names the output directory; reusing a name resumes that run.
rows.above: This sentinel is a reminder to choose a real run name. If there is already a checkpoint under this run, that checkpoint will auto-resume.  NOTE: Some unit/integration tests in MaxText do not always run this file directly. When running in decoupled mode (DECOUPLE_GCLOUD=TRUE), tests may use `decoupled_base_test.yml` instead of `base.yml` via `tests/utils/test_helpers.py`.

rows.what: Where checkpoints, metrics and logs go (a gs:// bucket in production; a local path here).
rows.above: Output directory Create a GCS bucket, e.g. my-maxtext-outputs and set this to "gs://my-maxtext-outputs/"

rows.what: '' , xplane (the JAX profiler) or nsys.
rows.comment: Supported profiler: '', xplane, nsys
rows.above: For nsys profiler, pass the training command to nsys command e.g. nsys profile -s none --force-overwrite true --capture-range=cudaProfilerApi --capture-range-end=stop {training command}

rows.what: Compile ahead of time for a named TPU topology (for example v5e-256) with train_compile.py; needs libtpu, so not run here.
rows.comment: Target hardware version, e.g. 'v5e-256'

rows.what: Persistent compilation cache directory.
rows.above: Jax cache directory

rows.what: How often metrics are flushed.
rows.comment: The frequency of Tensorboard flush, gcs metrics writing, and managed profiler metrics updating.
